effect_estimate.comment: Provided full text is truncated at PDF p. 70 of 216 (inside Section 4.4, p. 56), so quantitative Phase 2 household survey ANOVA/linear regression coefficients and physical water flow/tank tables in Chapters 5–8 (pp. 60–166) are not accessible in the excerpt. Extracted findings reflect only empirical/institutional results explicitly printed in PDF pp. 1–70.
effect_estimate.value: In Ukerewe District, only 36% of the rural population has safe and clean water supply (108 improved natural wells, 285 shallow wells, 3 taps), leaving villagers reliant on traditional micro spring forest water sources. On Ukerewe main Island, statutory formalization mechanisms have not taken hold due to administrative, procedural, and cost barriers: zero registered Water User Associations (WUAs) or Water User Groups (WUGs) exist in the study sites because district registration and village-to-district by-law approval processes are complex and slow; most resource users hold no Certificate of Customary Right of Occupancy (Hati miliki ya kimila) due to high surveying costs and non-coverage; and the Lake Victoria Basin Water Board/Office and District Forest Department do not actively manage small micro spring sources (<1 ha). Consequently, water access and conservation are governed through institutional bricolage combining customary clan norms/taboos, informal well committees, external programme rules (e.g., HESAWA), and village councils as a last-resort dispute forum (quantitative regression/ANOVA estimates from the N=180 household survey in Chapters 5–8 were truncated beyond PDF p. 70).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Mixed-methods design appraised with MMAT has a maximum ceiling of 2 under CODEBOOK.md §9. Even within the accessible pages (PDF pp. 1–70), the study directly documents empirical operation of customary vs. statutory tenure, non-issuance of customary occupancy certificates, absence of registered WUAs/WUGs, slow by-law procedures, and village council fallback dispute resolution on Ukerewe main Island.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines customary vs. statutory land/water/forest/tree tenure and property rights, written occupancy certificates (Hati miliki ya kimila) and formal WUA/WUG/water-right registration (documentation), applicant surveying costs and water cost-recovery policies (fees), complex WUA registration and surveying steps (procedural_steps), slow multi-tier district approval of village water by-laws (delay), customary taboos/sanctions and formal enforcement against defaulters (sanction), decentralized community management via WUGs/well committees/PFM (participation), and multi-ministry/multi-tier sectoral fragmentation across water, land, health, and forestry authorities (institutional_fragmentation).

outcome_flags.comment: Explicitly studies household access to and distance from micro spring water sources and alternative water sources (water_access), local and institutional water quality criteria/chlorination (service_quality), daily water quantity fetched per household, tank volume, and flow rates (service_quantity), and wet/dry season flow seasonality and functional status of taps/tanks/pipes (service_reliability). District rural safe water supply coverage (36%) is also reported as context (service_coverage).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Genuine two-phase primary mixed-methods study combining qualitative ethnography/PRA/policy analysis (Phase 1) and a random-sample quantitative household survey (N=180) with ANOVA/linear regression and physical water/forest measurements (Phase 2).

sample_size.comment: All sampling details are explicitly reported in Chapter 3 (Sections 3.3–3.5 and Table 3.3).
sample_size.value: 6 micro spring forest cases across 4 villages (selected from 22 visited micro spring forests in 11 villages); 180 households in main structured survey (30 randomly sampled households per case, plus 10 pilot households in Nzuitaka); PRA focus groups of 10–15 participants per case plus village and district key informants
sample_size.where_found: PDF pp. 46–52 (Chapter 3, Sections 3.3–3.5, pp. 32–38; Table 3.1 & Table 3.3)

study_design.comment: Explicitly designed and operationalized as a two-phase mixed-methods comparative case study across 6 micro spring forests.
study_design.value: Mixed-methods comparative case study combining Phase 1 qualitative ethnography, Participatory Rural Appraisal (focus groups, resource mapping, Venn diagrams, trend/time lines, matrix ranking), key informant interviews, and policy/legal review (Jan 2007–Apr 2008) with Phase 2 cross-sectional random-sample household survey (ANOVA and linear regression), GPS spatial measurement, forest stand inventory, and physical water source measurement (May–Dec 2008)
